claim: Cas7-11 is a Type III-E CRISPR Cas effector that confers programmable RNA cleavage.
source: Cas7-11 is a Type III-E CRISPR Cas effector that confers programmable RNA cleavage and has potential applications in RNA interference.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known property of Cas7-11, supported by the broader scientific literature on this system.

claim: Cas7-11 has potential applications in RNA interference.
source: Cas7-11 is a Type III-E CRISPR Cas effector that confers programmable RNA cleavage and has potential applications in RNA interference.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future applications based on the properties of Cas7-11.

claim: Cas7-11 encodes a single polypeptide containing four Cas7- and one Cas11-like segments.
source: Cas7-11 encodes a single polypeptide containing four Cas7- and one Cas11-like segments that obscures the distinction between the multi-subunit Class 1 and the single-subunit Class-2 CRISPR Cas systems.
evidence: This is a known structural feature of Cas7-11 from prior characterization.

claim: The structure of Cas7-11 obscures the distinction between the multi-subunit Class 1 and the single-subunit Class-2 CRISPR Cas systems.
source: Cas7-11 encodes a single polypeptide containing four Cas7- and one Cas11-like segments that obscures the distinction between the multi-subunit Class 1 and the single-subunit Class-2 CRISPR Cas systems.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural organization of Cas7-11.

claim: A cryo-EM structure of active DiCas7-11 was determined at 2.82 Å resolution.
source: We report a cryo-EM (cryo-electron microscopy) structure of the active Cas7-11 from Desulfonema ishimotonii (DiCas7-11) that reveals the molecular basis for RNA processing and interference activities.
evidence: The structure determination is the primary experimental result of this study, with resolution stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: DiCas7-11 arranges its Cas7- and Cas11-like domains in an extended form that resembles the backbone made up by four Cas7 and one Cas11 subunits in multi-subunit enzymes.
source: DiCas7-11 arranges its Cas7- and Cas11-like domains in an extended form that resembles the backbone made up by four Cas7 and one Cas11 subunits in the multi-subunit enzymes.
evidence: This structural observation is derived from the cryo-EM structure and comparison with multi-subunit Type III systems, as shown in Figure 1.

claim: The backbone of DiCas7-11 contains evolutionarily different Cas7 and Cas11 domains compared to multi-subunit enzymes.
source: Unlike the multi-subunit enzymes, however, the backbone of DiCas7-11 contains evolutionarily different Cas7 and Cas11 domains, giving rise to their unique functionality.
evidence: This is inferred from structural and sequence comparisons between DiCas7-11 and multi-subunit Type III systems.

claim: The first Cas7-like domain nearly engulfs the last 15 direct repeat nucleotides in processing and recognition of the CRISPR RNA.
source: The first Cas7-like domain nearly engulfs the last 15 direct repeat nucleotides in processing and recognition of the CRISPR RNA, and its free-standing fragment retains most of the activity.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: A free-standing fragment of the first Cas7-like domain retains most of the RNA processing activity.
source: The first Cas7-like domain nearly engulfs the last 15 direct repeat nucleotides in processing and recognition of the CRISPR RNA, and its free-standing fragment retains most of the activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2c showing that fC7L.1 can process pre-crRNA.

claim: Both the second and the third Cas7-like domains mediate target RNA cleavage in a metal-dependent manner.
source: Both the second and the third Cas7-like domains mediate target RNA cleavage in a metal-dependent manner.
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural analysis (Figure 3a) and biochemical assays showing EDTA inhibition (Figure 3c).

claim: The long variable insertion to the fourth Cas7 domain has little impact on RNA processing or targeting.
source: The structure and mutational data indicate that the long variable insertion to the fourth Cas7 domain has little impact on RNA processing or targeting, suggesting the possibility for engineering a compact and programmable RNA interference tool.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the DiCas7-11-Δint1 deletion mutant retaining activity in Figure 4c.

claim: The insertion domain deletion suggests the possibility for engineering a compact and programmable RNA interference tool.
source: The structure and mutational data indicate that the long variable insertion to the fourth Cas7 domain has little impact on RNA processing or targeting, suggesting the possibility for engineering a compact and programmable RNA interference tool.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the experimental observation that the insertion can be deleted without loss of function.

claim: Type III-A (Csm) and III-B (Cmr) subtypes assemble 4–5 Cas7, 2–3 Cas11, and 1 Cas10 subunits into a sea horse-shaped helical enzyme.
source: The multi-subunit Type III effectors, exemplified by the Type III-A (Csm) and the III-B subtypes (Cmr), assemble 4–5 Cas7, 2–3 Cas11, and 1 Cas10 subunits into a sea horse-shaped helical enzyme (Molina et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited reference.

claim: Type III effectors cleave target RNA at a 6-nucleotide interval within the complementary region.
source: They cleave the target RNA at a 6-nucleotide (nt) interval within the complementary region that coincides with the evenly spaced Cas7 subunits (Elmore et al., 2016; Samai et al., 2015; Tamulaitis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited references.

claim: Type VI (Cas13) is a single subunit effector that is substantially smaller than Type III effectors.
source: The Type VI, or Cas13, is a single subunit and substantially smaller effector.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Cas13 systems.

claim: Cas13 employs two higher eukaryotic and prokaryotic nucleotide binding domains in cleaving target RNA outside the complementary region.
source: Unlike Csm/Cmr, Cas13 employs two higher eukaryotic and prokaryotic nucleotide binding domains in cleaving the target RNA outside the complementary region (Abudayyeh et al., 2016; East-Seletsky et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited references.

claim: Cas7-11 is also known as gRAMP (giant repeat-associated mysterious protein).
source: The recently discovered Type III-E effector, Cas7-11 or gRAMP (for giant repeat-associated mysterious protein), is also a single subunit effector with fused Cas7-like and Cas11-like segments (van Beljouw et al., 2021; Özcan et al., 2021; Figure 1a).
evidence: This is an alternative name for Cas7-11 from the cited references.

claim: Cas7-11 employs Cas7-like segments to cleave crRNA-guided target RNA, similar to Csm/Cmr but unlike Cas13.
source: Unlike Cas13 but similar to Csm/Cmr, Cas7-11 employs the Cas7-like segments to cleave crRNA-guided target RNA (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is established from prior characterization cited in the references.

claim: Cas13 can distinguish self from foreign RNA by utilizing the 3' protospacer flanking sequence (PFS) in the target RNA.
source: Interestingly, whereas Cas13 can distinguish self from foreign RNA by utilizing the 3' protospacer flanking sequence (PFS) in the target RNA (Meeske and Marraffini, 2018), both Csm/Cmr and Cas7-11 are insensitive to 3' PFS in cleaving their respective target RNA (van Beljouw et al., 2021; Özcan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited reference.

claim: Both Csm/Cmr and Cas7-11 are insensitive to 3' PFS in cleaving their respective target RNA.
source: Interestingly, whereas Cas13 can distinguish self from foreign RNA by utilizing the 3' protospacer flanking sequence (PFS) in the target RNA (Meeske and Marraffini, 2018), both Csm/Cmr and Cas7-11 are insensitive to 3' PFS in cleaving their respective target RNA (van Beljouw et al., 2021; Özcan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established from the cited references.

claim: Csm/Cmr utilize an independent processing endonuclease, Cas6, to result in a mature crRNA containing an 8-nt repeat (5'-tag) linked to the spacer.
source: Csm/Cmr utilize an independent processing endonuclease, Cas6, to result in a mature crRNA containing an 8-nt repeat (5'-tag) linked to the spacer (Carte et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited reference.

claim: Both Cas13 and Cas7-11 process their own crRNA.
source: By contrast, both Cas13 and Cas7-11 process their own crRNA (East-Seletsky et al., 2016; van Beljouw et al., 2021; Özcan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established from the cited references.

claim: Cas7-11 is believed to be a unique Type III CRISPR-Cas system.
source: Cas7-11 is therefore believed to be a unique Type III CRIPSR-Cas system.
evidence: This is an inference based on the distinctive properties of Cas7-11 compared to other Type III systems.

claim: Cas7-11 has been demonstrated to form a complex with the caspase-like TPR-CHAT peptidase.
source: Interestingly, Cas7-11 has been demonstrated to form a complex with the caspase-like TPR-CHAT peptidase, suggesting a potential for a viral RNA-induced and protease-mediated antiviral immunity (van Beljouw et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established from the cited reference.

claim: The Cas7-11-TPR-CHAT complex suggests a potential for viral RNA-induced and protease-mediated antiviral immunity.
source: Interestingly, Cas7-11 has been demonstrated to form a complex with the caspase-like TPR-CHAT peptidase, suggesting a potential for a viral RNA-induced and protease-mediated antiviral immunity (van Beljouw et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed complex formation.

claim: Cas13 has collateral nuclease activity.
source: Given the known collateral nuclease activities of Cas13 (Abudayyeh et al., 2016; East-Seletsky et al., 2016) and Csm/Cmr (Elmore et al., 2016; Samai et al., 2015; Kazlauskiene et al., 2016), and the complex enzyme composition of Csm/Cmr, Cas7-11 provides a desirable platform to further develop RNA interference and editing tools.
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited references.

claim: Csm/Cmr have collateral nuclease activities.
source: Given the known collateral nuclease activities of Cas13 (Abudayyeh et al., 2016; East-Seletsky et al., 2016) and Csm/Cmr (Elmore et al., 2016; Samai et al., 2015; Kazlauskiene et al., 2016), and the complex enzyme composition of Csm/Cmr, Cas7-11 provides a desirable platform to further develop RNA interference and editing tools.
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited references.

claim: Cas7-11 provides a desirable platform to develop RNA interference and editing tools.
source: Given the known collateral nuclease activities of Cas13 (Abudayyeh et al., 2016; East-Seletsky et al., 2016) and Csm/Cmr (Elmore et al., 2016; Samai et al., 2015; Kazlauskiene et al., 2016), and the complex enzyme composition of Csm/Cmr, Cas7-11 provides a desirable platform to further develop RNA interference and editing tools.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the properties of Cas7-11 compared to other systems.

claim: DiCas7-11 has been demonstrated to function in programmable RNA cleavage and editing both in vitro and in mammalian cells.
source: DiCas7-11 has been demonstrated to function in programmable RNA cleavage and editing both in vitro and in mammalian cells (van Beljouw et al., 2021; Özcan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established from the cited references.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of DiCas7-11 was determined at an overall resolution of 2.82 Å.
source: To understand the molecular basis for crRNA processing and target interference by Cas7-11, we determined a cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of Desulfonema ishimotonii Cas7-11 (DiCas7-11) at an overall resolution of 2.82 Å (Figure 1b-c, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is the primary experimental result, with resolution shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The density map resolves most of the DiCas7-11 protein, the crRNA (–15 to +19) and the partially cleaved target RNA (+19* to +2*).
source: The density map resolves most of the DiCas7-11 protein, the crRNA (–15 to +19) and the partially cleaved target RNA (+19* to +2*) (Figure 1b-c, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM density map shown in the figures.

claim: The PFS region plus the first base paired nucleotide (+1*) are not observed in the structure.
source: The PFS region plus the first base paired nucleotide (+1*) are not observed.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The core Cas7-11 assembly is half-moon shaped with four Cas7-like (C7L) domains forming a long ridge and a single Cas11-like domain (C11L) occupying the crescent center.
source: The core Cas7-11 assembly is half-moon shaped with four Cas7-like (C7L) domains (C7L.1–C7L.4 from N- to the C-terminus) forming a long ridge and a single Cas11-like domain (C11L) occupying the crescent center.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The entire DiCas7-11 complex can be superimposed onto the Lactococcus lactis Csm (LlCsm) complex.
source: The entire DiCas7-11 complex can be superimposed onto the closely matched homologous Lactococcus lactis Csm (LlCsm) complex (Sridhara et al., 2022) (Type III-A) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4a) with the C7L.1-C7L.4 ridge matching that formed by four Cas7-like (Csm3) subunits and C11L matching the Cas11-like (Csm2) subunit adjacent to Cas10 (Csm1) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural superposition shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The similarity in the bound RNA trajectory at the core between DiCas7-11 and LlCsm is striking.
source: The similarity in the bound RNA trajectory at the core between the two complex is striking (Figure 1—figure supplement 4b), suggesting a similar RNA binding apparatus in both complexes.
evidence: This is observed from structural comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4b.

claim: DiCas7-11 and LlCsm have a similar RNA binding apparatus.
source: The similarity in the bound RNA trajectory at the core between the two complex is striking (Figure 1—figure supplement 4b), suggesting a similar RNA binding apparatus in both complexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural similarity in RNA binding.

claim: DiCas7-11 lacks the domains equivalent to the Csm4 and the Cas10 (Csm1) subunits.
source: DiCas7-11 lacks the domains equivalent to the Csm4 and the Cas10 (Csm1) subunits and, thus, the functions associated with them.
evidence: This is observed from structural comparison with LlCsm.

claim: DiCas7-11 lacks the functions associated with Csm4 and Cas10 subunits.
source: DiCas7-11 lacks the domains equivalent to the Csm4 and the Cas10 (Csm1) subunits and, thus, the functions associated with them.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of these structural domains.

claim: In Csm complexes, Csm4 recognizes and stabilizes the 8-nt 5'-tag derived from the direct repeat.
source: In Csm complexes, Csm4 recognizes and stabilizes the 8-nt 5'-tag derived from the direct repeat whereas Cas10 carries out cyclic oligoadenylate synthesis and ancillary DNA cleavage (Sridhara et al., 2022; You et al., 2019; Jia et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited references.

claim: Cas10 carries out cyclic oligoadenylate synthesis and ancillary DNA cleavage in Csm complexes.
source: In Csm complexes, Csm4 recognizes and stabilizes the 8-nt 5'-tag derived from the direct repeat whereas Cas10 carries out cyclic oligoadenylate synthesis and ancillary DNA cleavage (Sridhara et al., 2022; You et al., 2019; Jia et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited references.

claim: Cas10 secures the 3' PFS of the cognate target RNA and plays a role in discrimination of self from foreign RNA.
source: Cas10 also secures the 3' PFS of the cognate target RNA, and thus, plays a role in discrimination of self from foreign RNA (Sridhara et al., 2022; You et al., 2019; Jia et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited references.

claim: Wild-type DiCas7-11 successfully processes pre-crRNA and cleaves target RNA under reactive conditions.
source: Under this condition, DiCas7-11 successfully processes the pre-crRNA and cleaves the target RNA (Figure 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in the figures showing processing and cleavage products.

claim: The 34-nt crRNA lies along the C7L ridge with its repeat region spanning C7L.1-C7L.2 and the spacer region covering C7L.3-C7L.4.
source: The 34-nt crRNA lies along the C7L ridge with its repeat region spanning C7L.1-C7L.2 and the spacer region covering C7L.3-C7L.4 (Figure 1b-c and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in the figures.

claim: The first 18 nucleotides of the target RNA (+19* to +2*) remain base paired with the spacer region of the crRNA.
source: The first 18 nucleotides of the target RNA (+19* to +2*) remain base paired with the spacer region of the crRNA (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in the figures.

claim: The short span of the guide-target region on C7L domains explains the two, instead of four as in LlCsm, sites of target cleavage.
source: The short span of the guide-target region on C7L domains explains the two, instead of four as in LlCsm, sites of target cleavage (van Beljouw et al., 2021; Özcan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is inferred from structural observations and comparison with LlCsm.

claim: The pre-crRNA is processed by the first C7L domain, yielding a mature crRNA containing the last 15 nucleotides of the direct repeat (5'-tag) linked to the programmed spacer.
source: The observed structure suggests that the pre-crRNA is processed by the first C7L domain, which yields a mature crRNA containing the last 15 nucleotides of the direct repeat (5'-tag) linked to the programmed spacer (Figure 1c, Figure 2a, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is inferred from the structure and confirmed by biochemical assays in Figure 2.

claim: Synthetic pre-crRNA containing 2'-deoxy modification at −16, −15, or −14 position confirms cleavage products consistent with a 15-nt 5'-tag.
source: To confirm the site of processing, we subjected synthetic pre-crRNA containing 2'-deoxy modification at −16,–15, or –14 position to the processing reaction, respectively, and found that the cleavage products are consistent with the density-derived 15-nt 5'-tag (Figure 2b and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2b.

claim: The sequence identity upstream of U(–15) is not important for processing.
source: Strikingly, the sequence identity upstream of U(–15) is not important for processing, as those substituted with poly-adenine (polyA) or the previously characterized Candidatus Scalindua broadae (Csb) pre-crRNA are successfully processed by DiCas7-11 (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2c.

claim: His43 is immediately next to the leaving 5'-hydroxyl oxygen (2.3 Å) of U(–15), suggesting its role in processing.
source: A well-conserved histidine residue, His43, is immediately next to the leaving 5'-hydroxyl oxygen (2.3 Å) of U(–15), suggesting its role in processing.
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 2a and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: His43 to alanine mutation (H43A) abolished pre-crRNA cleavage.
source: Consistently, His43 to alanine mutation (H43A) abolished pre-crRNA cleavage (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2c.

claim: DiCas7-11 employs a general acid-base catalysis mechanism for processing, similar to Cas6.
source: The requirement for His43 without requiring divalent metals in processing suggests that DiCas7-11 employs a general acid-base catalysis mechanism similarly suggested for Cas6 (Li, 2015; Hochstrasser and Doudna, 2015), although detailed roles of His43 and other possible catalytic residues remain to be characterized.
evidence: This is inferred from the His43 requirement and comparison with Cas6 mechanism from cited references.

claim: The histidine-mediated processing reaction may be further assisted by nearby polar residues Tyr55 and Arg26.
source: In this regard, the histidine-mediated processing reaction may be further assisted by nearby polar residues Tyr55 (4.3 Å from the leaving 5'-hydroxyl oxygen) and Arg26 (5.1 Å from the leaving 5'-hydroxyl oxygen).
evidence: This is speculated based on the proximity of these residues to the cleavage site.

claim: CsbCas7-11 contains threonine in place of His43 and phenylalanine in place of Tyr55.
source: Interestingly, CsbCas7-11 contains threonine in place of His43 and phenylalanine in place of Tyr55, and it does not process its crRNA at position –15 (van Beljouw et al., 2021), suggesting that precise processing may not be required for the RNA interference activity.
evidence: This is established from the cited reference.

claim: CsbCas7-11 does not process its crRNA at position –15.
source: Interestingly, CsbCas7-11 contains threonine in place of His43 and phenylalanine in place of Tyr55, and it does not process its crRNA at position –15 (van Beljouw et al., 2021), suggesting that precise processing may not be required for the RNA interference activity.
evidence: This is established from the cited reference.

claim: Precise processing may not be required for RNA interference activity.
source: Interestingly, CsbCas7-11 contains threonine in place of His43 and phenylalanine in place of Tyr55, and it does not process its crRNA at position –15 (van Beljouw et al., 2021), suggesting that precise processing may not be required for the RNA interference activity.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that CsbCas7-11 functions without precise processing.

claim: The processed 15-nt 5'-tag interacts extensively with C7L.1 and to less extent with C7L.2.
source: The processed 15-nt 5'-tag interacts extensively with C7L.1 and to less extent with C7L.2 (Figure 2a and Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in the figures.

claim: The protein nearly buries the entire 5'-tag and thus precluded it from complete base pairing with a complementary RNA.
source: The protein nearly buries the entire 5'-tag and thus precluded it from complete base pairing with a complementary RNA.
evidence: This is observed in the structure.

claim: Well-conserved residues form base-specific interactions while non-conserved residues maintain interactions with RNA sugar phosphate backbone.
source: In general, well-conserved residues form base-specific interactions while non-conserved residues maintain interactions with RNA sugar phosphate backbone.
evidence: This is a general pattern observed in the structure.

claim: C7L.1 forms a ferredoxin fold (β2↑β3↓α2β1↑α1β4↓) highly abundant in CRISPR Cas components.
source: C7L.1 forms a ferredoxin fold (β2↑β3↓α2β1↑α1β4↓) highly abundant in CRISPR Cas components (Makarova et al., 2011; Wang and Li, 2012).
evidence: This is observed in the structure and is established knowledge from the cited references.

claim: C7L.1 uses α1, β2, a long β-hairpin connecting β2 to β3 (thumb) and a C7L.1-specific insertion loop (finger) to secure the significantly bent 5'-tag, resembling a rope-gripping right hand.
source: It uses α1, β2, a long β-hairpin connecting β2 to β3 (thumb) and a C7L.1-specific insertion loop (finger) to secure the significantly bent 5'-tag, resembling a rope-gripping right hand (Figure 2a and Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in the figures.

claim: The first nucleotide, U(–15), forms a hydrogen bond network with a number of residues including the well-conserved His43.
source: The first nucleotide, U(–15), forms a hydrogen bond network with a number of residues including the well-conserved His43 (Figure 2a, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in the figures.

claim: Removal of U(–15) did not impact target RNA cleavage.
source: Removal of U(–15) did not impact target RNA cleavage (Figure 2d), suggesting the possibility that the U(–15)-protein interactions may be important for processing rather than target interference.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2d.

claim: The U(–15)-protein interactions may be important for processing rather than target interference.
source: Removal of U(–15) did not impact target RNA cleavage (Figure 2d), suggesting the possibility that the U(–15)-protein interactions may be important for processing rather than target interference.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that U(–15) removal does not affect cleavage.

claim: The most extensive interactions take place at the strictly conserved A(–12)-U(–11)-G(–10)-U(–9) tetranucleotide.
source: The most extensive interactions take place at the strictly conserved A(–12)-U(–11)-G(–10)-U(–9) tetranucleotide (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Both sidechain and mainchain atoms of C7L.1 participate in 'reading' the four RNA bases of the AUGU tetranucleotide.
source: Both sidechain as well as mainchain atoms of C7L.1 participate in 'reading' the four RNA bases, and the amino acids involving base-specific contacts (Thr59, Arg62, Arg67, Lys89, Thr92, and Glu93) are well conserved (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in the structure and sequence alignment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: All edges of G(–10) (Watson-Crick, Hoogsteen, and sugar) are in close contacts with conserved C7L.1 residues.
source: Strikingly, all edges of G(–10), the Watson-Crick, the Hoogsteen, and the sugar, are in close contacts with the conserved C7L.1 residues (Figure 2a, Figure 1—figure supplement 5, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in the figures.

claim: Downstream of the AUGU tetranucleotide is a tight right-handed helical turn formed by C(–8)-A(–7)-C(–6)-G(–5).
source: Downstream of the AUGU tetranucleotide is a tight right-handed helical turn formed by C(–8)-A(–7)-C(–6)-G(–5).
evidence: This is observed in the structure.

claim: The tight turn is stabilized by both base stacking and an unusual network of intra-strand polar contacts.
source: The turn is stabilized by both base stacking as well as an unusual network of intra-strand polar contacts.
evidence: This is observed in the structure.

claim: The base of G(–5) interdigitates those of C(–8) and A(–7) with the well-conserved Arg35 on top, leaving C(–6) protruding into the interior of the protein.
source: The base of G(–5) interdigitates those of C(–8) and A(–7) with the well-conserved Arg35 on top, leaving C(–6) protruding into the interior of the protein (Figure 2a, Figure 1—figure supplement 5, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in the figures.

claim: Phosphate backbone atoms in A form RNA do not engage in intra-strand contacts.
source: Whereas phosphate backbone atoms in A form RNA do not engage in intra-strand contacts, those within the turn mediate numerous interactions (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is established knowledge about A-form RNA structure.

claim: Phosphate backbone atoms within the tight turn mediate numerous interactions.
source: Whereas phosphate backbone atoms in A form RNA do not engage in intra-strand contacts, those within the turn mediate numerous interactions (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The strictly conserved G(–5) forms the most intra-strand interactions.
source: The strictly conserved G(–5) forms the most intra-strand interactions.
evidence: This is observed in the structure.

claim: G(–5) N2 atom contacts the non-bridging oxygen of A(–7).
source: Its N2 atom contacts the non-bridging oxygen of A(–7) while its non-bridging oxygen forms hydrogen bond with 2'-OH of C(–8) (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 2a.

claim: G(–5) non-bridging oxygen forms hydrogen bond with 2'-OH of C(–8).
source: Its N2 atom contacts the non-bridging oxygen of A(–7) while its non-bridging oxygen forms hydrogen bond with 2'-OH of C(–8) (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The 2'-OH of G(–5) forms bifurcated contacts with the N7 atom of A(–7) and G(–4).
source: Finally, the 2'-OH of G(–5) forms bifurcated contacts with the N7 atom of the strictly conserved A(–7) and G(–4).
evidence: This is observed in the structure.

claim: The tight turn and the N+3 interactions involving the C(–8)-A(–7)-C(–6)-G(–5) backbone atoms is reminiscent of those within a 310 helix in proteins.
source: The tight and the N+3 interactions involving the C(–8)-A(–7)-C(–6)-G(–5) backbone atoms is reminiscent of those within a 310 helix in proteins.
evidence: This is an analogy drawn from structural observations.

claim: The non-conserved 5'-tag nucleotides A(–3), C(–6), and C(–8) form minimal contacts with the protein.
source: Interestingly, the non-conserved 5'-tag nucleotides, A(–3), C(–6), and C(–8) form minimal contacts with the protein, suggesting their minor roles in maintaining protein-RNA interactions (Figure 2a, Figure 1—figure supplement 5, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in the figures.

claim: Non-conserved 5'-tag nucleotides have minor roles in maintaining protein-RNA interactions.
source: Interestingly, the non-conserved 5'-tag nucleotides, A(–3), C(–6), and C(–8) form minimal contacts with the protein, suggesting their minor roles in maintaining protein-RNA interactions (Figure 2a, Figure 1—figure supplement 5, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the minimal contacts observed.

claim: The rest of the 5'-tag is clamped down by the thumb of C7L.1 and α1 of C7L.2 analogously as by two Cas7 subunits in Csm complexes.
source: The rest of the 5'-tag is clamped down by the thumb of C7L.1 and α1 of C7L.2 analogously as by two Cas7 subunits in Csm complexes (Sridhara et al., 2022).
evidence: This is observed in the structure and compared to Csm complexes from the cited reference.

claim: Removal of either first four or eight 5'-tag nucleotides abolished RNA-guided target cleavage.
source: Consistent with the extensive 5'-tag-protein interactions, removal of either first four or eight 5'-tag nucleotides abolished RNA-guided target cleavage (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2d.

claim: The different mode of 5'-tag binding to Cas7-11 from that of Csm explains the lack of a Cas10-like effector as in Csm.
source: The different mode of 5'-tag binding to Cas7-11 from that of Csm explains the lack of a Cas10-like effector as in Csm.
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison.

claim: Cas7-11 allosterically activates the TPR-CHAT protease in a 3' PFS-dependent manner.
source: Rather, it allosterically activates a different effector, the TPR-CHAT protease, in a 3' PFS-dependent manner.
evidence: This is established from prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: The last two 5'-tag nucleotides, C(–1) and A(–2), are partially solvent-accessible and can potentially participate in PFS-mediated activation of the TRP-CHAT activity.
source: Though 13 of the 15 5'-tag nucleotides are buried by the protein, the last two, C(–1) and A(–2), are partially solvent-accessible and can potentially participate in PFS-mediated activation of the TRP-CHAT activity (Hu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is inferred from structural observations and cited reference.

claim: A free-standing C7L.1 (fC7L.1) domain may be sufficient for binding and processing pre-crRNA.
source: Based on structural observations, we hypothesized that a free-standing C7L.1 (fC7L.1) domain may be sufficient for binding and processing pre-crRNA.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural observations.

claim: A truncated mutant comprised of residues 1–238 (fC7L.1) was created and purified.
source: We thus created and purified a truncated mutant comprised of residues 1–238 (hereafter fC7L.1 for free C7L.1) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is an experimental procedure described in the text and shown in the figure.

claim: fC7L.1 successfully processed pre-crRNA, albeit at slightly reduced efficiency compared to wild-type DiCas7-11.
source: Following 30 min incubation with pre-cRNA, fC7L.1 successfully processed the RNA, albeit at slightly reduced efficiency as compared to wild-type DiCas7-11 (Figure 2c, right).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2c.

claim: fC7L.1 remains bound to the cleaved pre-crRNA specifically.
source: In addition, electrophoretic mobility shift assay shows that fC7L.1 remains bound to the cleaved pre-crRNA specifically (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b), suggesting its potential to be used as a new CRISPR tool for in vivo RNA tracking or purification.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b.

claim: fC7L.1 has potential to be used as a new CRISPR tool for in vivo RNA tracking or purification.
source: In addition, electrophoretic mobility shift assay shows that fC7L.1 remains bound to the cleaved pre-crRNA specifically (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b), suggesting its potential to be used as a new CRISPR tool for in vivo RNA tracking or purification.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed binding activity.

claim: The spacer region of the crRNA is captured by the rest of the C7L ridge and base paired with the target RNA.
source: The spacer region of the crRNA is captured by the rest of the C7L ridge and base paired with the target RNA (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The three base paired regions largely resemble A form helix with some deviations in base-pair tilt.
source: The three base paired regions largely resemble A form helix with some deviations in base-pair tilt (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3b.

claim: Three of the four C7L domains contain the characteristic 'thumb' that secure the crRNA at two evenly spaced (6-nt) kinks with bases flipped.
source: Three of the four C7L domains contain the characteristic 'thumb' that secure the crRNA at two evenly spaced (6-nt) kinks with bases flipped.
evidence: This is observed in the structure.

claim: The duplex bound by C7L.4 creates an extra spacing between the G(+13*)-C(+13) and G(+14*)-C(+14) pairs but no base flipping.
source: The duplex bound by C7L.4 creates an extra spacing between the G(+13*)-C(+13) and G(+14*)-C(+14) pairs but no base flipping.
evidence: This is observed in the structure.

claim: The kinked crRNA-target RNA duplex creates bended sugar-phosphate backbone at the locations that coincide with the sites of cleavage.
source: Like the multi-subunit Type III effectors, the kinked crRNA-target RNA duplex creates bended sugar-phosphate backbone at the locations that coincide with the sites of cleavage.
evidence: This is observed in the structure.

claim: Both cleavage sites are cleaved by Cas7-11 in a metal-dependent manner.
source: Both sites are cleaved by Cas7-11 in a metal-dependent manner (Figure 3b and c).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3b and c showing EDTA inhibition.

claim: Type III systems generate 2',3'-cyclic product in spite of metal dependence.
source: Consistent with the previous observation that Type III systems generate 2',3'-cyclic product in spite of the metal dependence (Hale et al., 2009), the target RNA containing 2'-deoxy modification at A(+4*) (site 1) and C (+10*) (site 2) prevented formation of any cleavage product (Figure 3b and d).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited reference.

claim: Target RNA containing 2'-deoxy modification at A(+4*) (site 1) and C(+10*) (site 2) prevented formation of any cleavage product.
source: Consistent with the previous observation that Type III systems generate 2',3'-cyclic product in spite of the metal dependence (Hale et al., 2009), the target RNA containing 2'-deoxy modification at A(+4*) (site 1) and C (+10*) (site 2) prevented formation of any cleavage product (Figure 3b and d).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3b and d.

claim: Asp429 and Asp654 were previously shown to be critical to cleavage at site 1 and site 2, respectively.
source: Two acidic residues, Asp429 and Asp654, were previously shown to be critical to cleavage at site 1 and site 2, respectively (Özcan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established from the cited reference.

claim: Asp429 and Asp654 are found near each corresponding scissile phosphate with the carboxylate oxygen 4.2–6.7 Å from the leaving 5'-oxygen.
source: Satisfactorily, they are found near each corresponding scissile phosphate with the carboxylate oxygen 4.2–6.7 Å from the leaving 5'-oxygen (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 3a.

claim: At both cleavage sites, the phosphodiester bond breakage is further assisted by the near 'in-line' geometry of the nucleophilic 2'-oxygen, the scissile phosphate and the leaving 5'-oxygen.
source: At both sites, the phosphodiester bond breakage is further assisted by the near 'in-line' geometry of the nucleophilic 2'-oxygen, the scissile phosphate and the leaving 5'-oxygen (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Arg283 (site 1) and His306 (site 2) from the C11L domain stabilize the attacking nucleotides by stacking on their bases.
source: Two residues from the C11L domain, Arg283 (site 1) and His306 (site 2), where Arg283 is better conserved than His306, are observed to stabilize the attacking nucleotides by stacking on their bases (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 3a.

claim: No sufficient density is observed that can be assigned to Mg2+ ions despite demonstrated dependence on Mg2+ in target cleavage.
source: Despite the demonstrated dependence on Mg2+ in target cleavage (Figure 3c), no sufficient density is observed that can be assigned to Mg2+ ions.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The roles of protein residues in facilitating metal-dependent phosphodiester bond breakage remain unclear.
source: The roles of these protein residues in facilitating metal-dependent phosphodiester bond breakage remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current limitation in understanding the mechanism.

claim: In CsbCas7-11, Asp429 is not conserved and mutation of its equivalent Asp448 and other surrounding residues did not impact site 1 cleavage.
source: Interestingly in the homologous CsbCas7-11, Asp429 is not conserved and mutation of its equivalent Asp448 and other surrounding residues did not impact site 1 cleavage (van Beljouw et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established from the cited reference.

claim: Tyr360 is not required for site 1 cleavage in DiCas7-11.
source: Surprisingly, we found that Tyr360 is not required for site 1 cleavage (Figure 3b and f), indicating that, at least for DiCas7-11, Asp429 is sufficient in mediating the metal-dependent cleavage.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3b and f.

claim: For DiCas7-11, Asp429 is sufficient in mediating the metal-dependent cleavage at site 1.
source: Surprisingly, we found that Tyr360 is not required for site 1 cleavage (Figure 3b and f), indicating that, at least for DiCas7-11, Asp429 is sufficient in mediating the metal-dependent cleavage.
evidence: This is inferred from the Tyr360 mutation experiment.

claim: As short as 16 base pairs in total length and 2 base pairs on one flanking end can facilitate RNA cleavage.
source: We found that as short of 16 base pairs in total length and 2 base pairs on one flanking end can facilitate RNA cleavage (Figure 3b and e), suggesting that both protein and crRNA:target pairing play significant roles in shaping the target RNA for cleavage.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3b and e.

claim: Both protein and crRNA:target pairing play significant roles in shaping the target RNA for cleavage.
source: We found that as short of 16 base pairs in total length and 2 base pairs on one flanking end can facilitate RNA cleavage (Figure 3b and e), suggesting that both protein and crRNA:target pairing play significant roles in shaping the target RNA for cleavage.
evidence: This is inferred from the truncation experiments.

claim: Focused classification and refinement led to a low-resolution map that matches the AlphaFold-predicted model of the insertion domain.
source: Though the final atomic model of DiCas7-11 lacks the large insertion to C7L.4 (residues 979–1297) due to weak density, focused classification and refinement led to a low-resolution map that matches the AlphaFold-predicted model of the insertion domain (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: This is described as a computational analysis result shown in Figure 4.

claim: A large majority of the insertion domain is not engaged with any of the features described for RNA processing or targeting.
source: This model indicates that a large majority of the insertion domain is not engaged with any of the features described above and suggests the possibility that it is not essential to RNA-guided target cleavage.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural model.

claim: The insertion domain is possibly not essential to RNA-guided target cleavage.
source: This model indicates that a large majority of the insertion domain is not engaged with any of the features described above and suggests the possibility that it is not essential to RNA-guided target cleavage.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural observations.

claim: DiCas7-11-Δint1 (with residues 1009–1220 removed) retains almost all RNA-guided target cleavage activity in vitro.
source: To test this hypothesis, we removed residues 1009–1220 to create DiCas7-11-Δint1. Consistently, we showed that DiCas7-11-Δint1 retains almost all RNA-guided target cleavage in an in vitro assay (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4c.

claim: A structure of catalytically inactive DiCas7-11 (Asp429 and Asp654 to alanine) bound with a slightly modified crRNA (U(–15) replaced by G(–15)) is available (PDB ID: 7WAH).
source: A structure of catalytically inactive DiCas7-11 (Asp429 and Asp654 to alanine) bound with a slightly modified crRNA (U(–15) is replaced by G(–15)) recently became available (PDB ID: 7WAH) (Kato et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established from the cited reference.

claim: The active form of DiCas7-11 bound with processed native crRNA shows close agreement in protein and RNA structures with the catalytically inactive form.
source: We superimposed the active form of DiCas7-11 bound with the processed native crRNA (this study) to that by Kato et al. (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) and found a close agreement in protein and RNA structures.
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural superposition shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The superimposed structures resulted in 0.918 Å r.m.s.d. for 8114 atoms for protein.
source: The superimposed structures resulted in 0.918 Å root-means-square-difference (r.m.s.d.) for 8114 atoms for protein, 0.691 Å for 192 backbone atoms of crRNA, and 0.80 Å for 96 backbone atoms of target, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3a.

claim: The target cleavage sites are highly similar between the active and inactive DiCas7-11 structures despite the mutated catalytic aspartates.
source: The target cleavage sites are highly similar despite the protein used by Kato et al., 2022, contains mutated catalytic aspartates.
evidence: This is observed from structural comparison.

claim: The largest difference between the two structures is observed in interactions between DiCas7-11 and the first 5'-tag residue.
source: The largest difference, however, is observed in interactions between DiCas7-11 and the first 5'-tag residue between the two structures.
evidence: This is observed from structural comparison.

claim: In the structure by Kato et al., G(–15) (non-native) establishes minimal interactions with the protein.
source: In that by Kato et al., G(–15), which is non-native, establishes minimal interactions with the protein, whereas in that of the active DiCas7-11, the native U(–15) interacts extensively with conserved protein residues (Figure 2a, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and Figure 2—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is observed from structural comparison shown in the figures.

claim: In the active DiCas7-11 structure, the native U(–15) interacts extensively with conserved protein residues.
source: In that by Kato et al., G(–15), which is non-native, establishes minimal interactions with the protein, whereas in that of the active DiCas7-11, the native U(–15) interacts extensively with conserved protein residues (Figure 2a, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and Figure 2—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in the figures.

claim: Catalytic His43 forms a close contact with the 5'-OH leaving group of U(–15) but is at a greater distance to G(–15).
source: In addition, whereas catalytic His43 forms a close contact with the 5'-OH leaving group of U(–15), it is at a greater distance to G(–15) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is observed in the structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3b.

claim: Though U(–15) is nonessential to the architecture and the target-cleavage competency of DiCas7-11, it may be important for efficient processing.
source: This result suggests that, though U(–15) is nonessential to the architecture and the target-cleavage competency of DiCas7-11, it may be important for efficient processing.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural comparison and biochemical data.

claim: The structure and complementary biochemical assays show that Cas7-11 has a minimal architecture required for programmable RNA cleavage.
source: The structure and complementary biochemical assays show that Cas7-11 has a minimal architecture required for programmable RNA cleavage.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the structural and biochemical data presented.

claim: The covalent linkage of the homologous units suggests an evolutionary advantage in dedicating Cas7-11 to RNA cleavage.
source: The covalent linkage of the homologous units suggests an evolutionary advantage in dedicating Cas7-11 to RNA cleavage.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about evolutionary implications.

claim: Cas7-11 offers a desirable alternative to Cas13 and Csm/Cmr in developing gene regulation tools.
source: Considering the known collateral RNase activity of Cas13 and the complicated Csm/Cmr systems, Cas7-11 offers a desirable alternative in developing gene regulation tools.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on comparison of different CRISPR systems.

claim: DiCas7-11 has been successfully demonstrated to function in mammalian cells.
source: While DiCas7-11 has been successfully demonstrated to function in mammalian cells, the efficiency and accuracy remain to be improved.
evidence: This is established from prior work.

claim: The efficiency and accuracy of DiCas7-11 in mammalian cells remain to be improved.
source: While DiCas7-11 has been successfully demonstrated to function in mammalian cells, the efficiency and accuracy remain to be improved.
evidence: This is a statement about current limitations.

claim: Protein engineering may assist efforts in designing improved Cas7-11-derived RNA interference platforms.
source: With now the available structures and the accurately mapped processing and target cleavage sites, protein engineering may assist the efforts in designing improved Cas7-11-derived RNA interference platforms.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future applications.

claim: Both fC7L.1 and DiCas7-11-Δint1 lend a proof-of-concept for engineering efforts.
source: Both fC7L.1 and DiCas7-11-Δint1 lend a proof-of-concept for such an effort.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental results with these variants.
